1.pericope_label: Give ear, O my people, to my law... that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes Maskil for a meditation or didactic poem, notes that the psalm's Asaphic origin has been contested, and links it to the psalm before by their closing images of a flock. Ellicott corrects 'my law' to 'instruction', and makes the handing down a command rather than a custom by reading the relative as temporal.

Calvin dates the psalm from its ending, long after David's death, since the ten tribes are already separated, and reads the title as a memorial David made against forgetting. Gill hears Christ speaking as 'King of the Jews, though they would not have him reign over them'.

Clarke brackets the date between the schism and the captivity, 'for the temple was still standing', and explains why a poem carries the history at all, since books were scarce and tradition was 'the only means of preserving the memory of past events'. Wesley shifts the difficulty of the 'dark sayings' from the words to the facts.

Henry insists the dark sayings are hard not to understand but to admire, and defends the strong word: 'every good truth, received in the light and love of it, will have the power of a law upon the conscience.' Spurgeon defends allegorical reading — 'the tribes and their marchings are living allegories' — and asks, 'shall God speak, and his children refuse to hear?'

Augustine reads the title as a summons to a particular kind of reader, one 'who doth perceive not the voice which the surface uttereth, but some inward sense', and distinguishes parables from propositions to forbid reading either cursorily.

positions.view: Not obscure but weighty: 'called dark sayings, not because they are hard to be understood, but because they are greatly to be admired and carefully to be looked into'.
The words are plain; the facts are incredible — the goodness and the ingratitude alike 'prodigious and hard to be believed'.
Genuinely requiring work: propositions 'are questions having something therein which is to be solved by disputation'.
Christ, claiming a people who rejected him.
David as king, or the psalmist as prophet 'as God's mouth' — the phrase pointing 'to a position of weight and authority'.

outliers.view: The only voice to explain the psalm's form from the technology of its age, as a chronological poem carrying history where books were too scarce to.

themes: Give ear, O my people, to my law: incline your ears to the words of my mouth.
I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old:
Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the Lord, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children:
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:
That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments:
And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God.

9.pericope_label: The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle... He brought streams also out of the rock

schools.summary: Ellicott proposes that no defeat is described at all: the Hebrew yields 'the sons of Ephraim are like men drawing slack bowstrings which turn back in the day of battle', freeing us 'from the necessity of conjecturing a particular incident'; and he explains the verse's position as a climax the poet could not keep back. He also identifies Zoan as Tanis, and asks whether the water came from boring 'through the rock to the great ocean on which the earth was supposed to rest'.

Gill measures how quickly the wonders were forgotten — within 'three days' journey in the wilderness' — takes the two rocks for real places 'both to be seen at this day', and reads the guiding cloud as a type of Christ.

Clarke lists the candidate defeats and refuses to choose among them; Wesley takes Ephraim as standing for all Israel and maps the psalm's structure, the disaster stated, its causes discoursed at length, and the history resumed at the sixtieth verse.

Henry draws the moral from the failure of equipment — 'weapons of war stand men in little stead without a martial spirit, and that is gone if God be gone' — and orders the two causes: 'our forgetfulness of God's works is at the bottom of our disobedience to his laws.'

debates.question: What defeat of Ephraim is meant?

positions.view: The Philistine rout in Eli's day, when the ark was taken.
Unknown. Candidates include the men of Gath and a defeat in the desert, but 'to what defeat of the Ephraimites this refers is not certainly known.'
None. The verse describes a slack bowstring recoiling, not soldiers retreating — a character, not an incident.

outliers.view: The only voice to dissolve the historical problem entirely by re-reading the verse as a simile about unreliable bows.

themes: The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle.
They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in his law;
And forgat his works, and his wonders that he had shewed them.
Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.
He divided the sea, and caused them to pass through; and he made the waters to stand as an heap.
In the daytime also he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a light of fire.
He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths.
He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers.

17.pericope_label: And they sinned yet more against him by provoking the most High in the wilderness... the wrath of God came upon them, and slew the fattest of them

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the discontent predated the water from the rock, keeps the popular 'angels' food' against the rival 'lordly food' since it suits 'food from heaven', and takes the winds as record rather than ornament — 'probably the very winds that brought the flights of quails' — while allowing 'poetical hyperbole' in the numbers.

Gill reconstructs the murmurers' reasoning as naturalism, the water perhaps having lain in the rock's caverns and come out of itself; he states the offence of unbelief formally, and condemns the eating as gluttony rather than hunger.

Clarke renders the request as meat 'for their lives' and judges the askers 'wholly carnal... earthly, animal, and devilish'; he explains the corn of heaven from its seed-like fall, and turns the unbelief on the present generation. Wesley separates need from 'inordinate and luxurious appetite'.

positions.view: The angels', literally: 'so called, because it was made by the ministry of angels'.
The mighty ones' — 'such bread as could only be expected at the tables of the rich and great', so that commoners ate what princes ate.
The lordly reading is possible, and would mean quails; but 'in connection with food from heaven, the popular idea of angels' food which poetry reluctantly gives up may be retained'.
Either 'the strongest or the noblest' — the word will bear both.
The strongest, and justly, since they 'probably were most desirous of this food, and fed most eagerly upon it'.

outliers.view: The only voice to put a naturalistic explanation into the murmurers' mouths, having them account for the water from the rock as groundwater that would have come out anyway.

themes: And they sinned yet more against him by provoking the most High in the wilderness.
And they tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust.
Yea, they spake against God; they said, Can God furnish a table in the wilderness?
Behold, he smote the rock, that the waters gushed out, and the streams overflowed; can he give bread also? can he provide flesh for his people?
Therefore the Lord heard this, and was wroth: so a fire was kindled against Jacob, and anger also came up against Israel;
Because they believed not in God, and trusted not in his salvation:
Though he had commanded the clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven,
And had rained down manna upon them to eat, and had given them of the corn of heaven.
Man did eat angels’ food: he sent them meat to the full.
He caused an east wind to blow in the heaven: and by his power he brought in the south wind.
He rained flesh also upon them as dust, and feathered fowls like as the sand of the sea:
And he let it fall in the midst of their camp, round about their habitations.
So they did eat, and were well filled: for he gave them their own desire;
They were not estranged from their lust. But while their meat was yet in their mouths,
The wrath of God came upon them, and slew the fattest of them, and smote down the chosen men of Israel.

32.pericope_label: For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works... he remembered that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away

schools.summary: Ellicott makes a change of tense that changes the doctrine: the verbs 'should be in the present, But he, the compassionate, forgives iniquity, and doth not destroy' — turning a fact about one generation into a description of God. He traces the Rock to the song of Moses.

Gill explains why the mercies failed of their effect, since unsanctified they 'often prove snares and temptations to sin yet more and more'; he offers two senses of 'flesh', frailty or corruption, and finds the tenderness of the divine compassion in a word cognate with the womb.

Clarke marvels that neither mercy nor judgment worked and then turns the marvel on the reader; he presses the kinsman-sense of the redeemer, reads the flattery through the Latin — 'they loved him with their mouth; and they lied unto him with their tongue' — and objects sharply to the English of the closing clause. Wesley calls the years 'tedious and fruitless marches hither and thither'.

debates.question: What does 'they were but flesh' concede?

positions.view: Frailty: 'poor, frail, weak, mortal creatures', unable to bear the weight of God's displeasure.
Or corruption: 'naturally sinful and corrupt, prone to evil' — mercy in either case.

debates.question: Does the wind that passes away deny a future life?

positions.view: The English suggests it and should be corrected: 'I believe this to be a bad translation and may be productive of error.' The Hebrew says 'the spirit goeth away, and it doth not return' — it does not return to probation, not that it ceases.

outliers.view: The only voice to change the tense of the mercy clause into the present, so that the verse describes God's standing character rather than one act of forbearance.

themes: For all this they sinned still, and believed not for his wondrous works.
Therefore their days did he consume in vanity, and their years in trouble.
When he slew them, then they sought him: and they returned and enquired early after God.
And they remembered that God was their rock, and the high God their redeemer.
Nevertheless they did flatter him with their mouth, and they lied unto him with their tongues.
For their heart was not right with him, neither were they stedfast in his covenant.
But he, being full of compassion, forgave their iniquity, and destroyed them not: yea, many a time turned he his anger away, and did not stir up all his wrath.
For he remembered that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again.

40.pericope_label: How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness... He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust

schools.summary: Ellicott counts the ten recorded murmurings, lays out five renderings of the disputed verb and settles for the plainest — 'the ideas of marking something that has been tried, and that of trying or tempting are sufficiently near to allow us to render tempted' — and warns that the plague-list 'is not a complete enumeration, and does not proceed in the order of the historic narrative'.

Gill notes that the whole period came to be named after the provocation, finds in the water turned to blood 'a just retaliation for drowning the infants of the Israelites in their river', and identifies the caterpillar with the locust of the next clause.

Clarke traces the disputed verb to a root meaning to mark, the same that named the letter which 'had the form of a cross X', and concludes that 'here it most obviously means an insult offered to God'. Wesley identifies the forgotten day as the deliverance from Pharaoh, and insists the flies and frogs were 'extraordinary in their nature'.

Henry distinguishes provoking from grieving, since God 'looked upon them as his children', and answers the presumption of limiting God out of the title itself. Spurgeon argues that the forgetting must have been practical rather than actual, since 'he who forgets the natural returns of gratitude, may justly be charged with not remembering the obligation'.

debates.question: What does it mean to have 'limited' the Holy One?

positions.view: To insult. The root means to mark or to sign, and here 'it most obviously means an insult offered to God'.
Simply to tempt. The renderings offered — branded, exasperated, crossed, thwarted — are near enough to trying that 'tempted' will serve.
To prescribe: fixing 'what proofs he should give of his power' and confining him 'to their way and their time'.

outliers.view: The only voice to notice how hard the forgetting would have been, and to resolve it by distinguishing practical from actual forgetfulness.

themes: How oft did they provoke him in the wilderness, and grieve him in the desert!
Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel.
They remembered not his hand, nor the day when he delivered them from the enemy.
How he had wrought his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Zoan:
And had turned their rivers into blood; and their floods, that they could not drink.
He sent divers sorts of flies among them, which devoured them; and frogs, which destroyed them.
He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust.

47.pericope_label: He destroyed their vines with hail... they provoked him to anger with their high places, and moved him to jealousy with their graven images

schools.summary: Ellicott meets an argument that the vines and sycamores betray 'a Palestinian rather than an Egyptian point of view' by citing the mural paintings, the wine offerings and a papyrus; he prefers a variant reading 'pestilence' for hail, removes the adjective from the evil angels, and returns to his earlier reading of the bow as relaxed rather than deceitful.

Gill hears a balance in the way made for the anger — God 'weighed it in the balance of justice, and proportioned his anger to their crimes' — and makes the leading out a study in helplessness, the people going 'like sheep, weak, timorous, unarmed'.

Clarke supplies the Egyptian detail, admits that of the evil angels 'what they were we cannot tell', and describes from experience the recurved bow that springs back and breaks the arm of whoever strings it badly. Wesley reads the angels as God's agents and the mountain as the highland of Canaan.

Spurgeon insists the deliverance was carried through to the end, God not leaving them 'halfway upon their journey'. Henry states the cost of the renewed rebellion: 'those whom the Lord forsakes become an easy prey to the destroyer.'

positions.view: Unknown, but severe. 'This is the first mention we have of evil angels'; they were 'the sorest plague that God had sent', and are not the destroying angel, whom the psalm names separately.
A mistranslation. The Hebrew has 'angels (or messengers) of ills', referring to the destruction of the firstborn.
Simply those 'whom God employed in producing these plagues'.
Zion, 'though from its apposition to border some prefer to take it of all the mountain country'.
The highland of Canaan at large, so called by contrast with Egypt, 'a long, continued, and almost perfect level'.

outliers.view: The only voice to answer a literary argument about the poem's standpoint with archaeological evidence, defeating the Palestinian hypothesis from Egyptian tomb paintings and a papyrus.

themes: He destroyed their vines with hail, and their sycomore trees with frost.
He gave up their cattle also to the hail, and their flocks to hot thunderbolts.
He cast upon them the fierceness of his anger, wrath, and indignation, and trouble, by sending evil angels among them.
He made a way to his anger; he spared not their soul from death, but gave their life over to the pestilence;
And smote all the firstborn in Egypt; the chief of their strength in the tabernacles of Ham:
But made his own people to go forth like sheep, and guided them in the wilderness like a flock.
And he led them on safely, so that they feared not: but the sea overwhelmed their enemies.
And he brought them to the border of his sanctuary, even to this mountain, which his right hand had purchased.
He cast out the heathen also before them, and divided them an inheritance by line, and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents.
Yet they tempted and provoked the most high God, and kept not his testimonies:
But turned back, and dealt unfaithfully like their fathers: they were turned aside like a deceitful bow.
For they provoked him to anger with their high places, and moved him to jealousy with their graven images.

59.pericope_label: When God heard this, he was wroth, and greatly abhorred Israel... So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands

schools.summary: Ellicott is the most exact on the unmourned widows, referring the clause 'undoubtedly' to the wife of Phinehas, who died in premature labour and so could not lament; he registers the boldness of likening God to a warrior flushed with wine, hedges the smiting of the enemies, corrects 'ewes great with young' to 'ewes with lambs', and admits the temple simile 'is vague'.

Gill keeps the fire figurative, dates the awaking to the smiting of the Philistines, reads the sanctuary as built unlike 'the high places, where idolatry was committed', and finds David's integrity in an administration that sought 'not his own honour and interest, but the good of his people'.

Clarke insists the forsaking of Shiloh was permanent — God 'never returned to it again' — supplies the eastern custom behind the unmarried maidens, unpacks the wine-flushed hero without flinching, and reports that some versions found a rhinoceros in the temple simile. Wesley finds the sharpest irony in the Philistines sending back the ark with their own golden emblems of shame.

Spurgeon weighs Ephraim's record before its rejection — Joshua, Gideon and Shiloh all belonged to it — and concludes that 'sin had been found in them, folly and instability, and therefore they were set aside as unfit to lead'.

debates.question: What was the sanctuary built like?

positions.view: Prominently: several versions read the word as the rhinoceros, the temple standing on Zion 'as the horn of the unicorn does upon his snout'.
The clause 'is vague'; perhaps 'high as heaven — firm as earth'.
Magnificently — and, for Gill, pointedly unlike 'the high places, where idolatry was committed'.

debates.question: How were the enemies smitten in the hinder parts?

positions.view: By the haemorrhoids that afflicted the Philistines while they held the ark — a shame they then published themselves in the golden emblems they returned with it.
Possibly that, 'or else the repeated defeats' of the Philistines under later kings.

outliers.view: The only voice to identify the unmourned widow precisely, and to prefer an older English version for catching what the received text loses.

themes: When God heard this, he was wroth, and greatly abhorred Israel:
So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men;
And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy’s hand.
He gave his people over also unto the sword; and was wroth with his inheritance.
The fire consumed their young men; and their maidens were not given to marriage.
Their priests fell by the sword; and their widows made no lamentation.
Then the Lord awaked as one out of sleep, and like a mighty man that shouteth by reason of wine.
And he smote his enemies in the hinder parts: he put them to a perpetual reproach.
Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim:
But chose the tribe of Judah, the mount Zion which he loved.
And he built his sanctuary like high palaces, like the earth which he hath established for ever.
He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds:
From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance.
So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands.
